summary: Defines terms used in discussing Internet Fax and describes the goals of the Internet Fax working group, setting a baseline of desired functionality against which proposed protocols can be judged. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2542 gives the Internet Fax working group shared terms and goals for evaluating protocol designs. It covers different ways to deliver a fax and ranks the importance of desired features.

questions: what is a fax onramp and offramp
what are the internet fax operational modes
what is store and forward fax
subtitle: Shared terminology and goals for evaluating Internet fax protocols.

tldr.problem: Several ways to send fax documents over the Internet existed, and the working group needed shared terms and a baseline for judging protocol proposals.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines Internet Fax roles and delivery modes, then states operational and functional goals with three priority levels.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2542 describes goals and desired functionality rather than specifying an Internet Fax protocol. It calls for interoperability, delivery confirmation, reliability and security.

facts.label: Roles described
facts.value: Network scanner, network printer, fax onramp and fax offramp

today: RFC 2542 is an Informational memo that defines goals and terminology for Internet Fax rather than a protocol. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Purpose and Priority Levels
sections.content:
Internet Fax means an application that approximates traditional fax while using Internet protocols for some part of the transmission. RFC 2542 defines terms and sets a baseline of desired functionality for protocols covering real-time, session and store-and-forward delivery.

Requirements use priority markers. {1} means a critical characteristic with general agreement; {2} marks a feature most participants consider important; and {3} marks a useful feature that other factors may override.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo sets goals against which Internet Fax proposals can be compared. Its priority markers show which goals are critical, important or useful.

sections.title: Devices, Roles and Delivery Modes
sections.content:
The memo separates Internet Fax roles that may be combined in one device: a network scanner, network printer, fax onramp gateway and fax offramp gateway. An onramp forwards a telephone fax call over the Internet; an offramp forwards an Internet transmission to a traditional fax terminal.

It describes three operational modes. Store-and-forward holds the document at one or more staging points before sending it onward. Session mode provides a delivery notification before disconnection and expects direct negotiation and retransmission. Real-time mode preserves essential T.30 exchanges with minimal added session time.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet Fax can connect scanners, printers, Internet hosts and traditional fax machines. It can store a document before forwarding it, keep a session open for delivery feedback, or carry a real-time fax exchange.

sections.title: Operational Goals
sections.content:
The protocol must support commonly used traditional fax features using Internet protocols and must allow compliant senders and recipients to interoperate. For delivery, the sender must be able to request a notification and receive a definite result: delivered, not delivered or no confirmation possible. Read confirmation is desirable but not required.

The memo also calls for quick delivery when requested, a minimum feature set that works across capable and less capable devices, reliability when capability information is outdated, and low processing demands. It says Internet Fax should reconcile fax's expectation of immediate delivery and confirmation with email's delayed delivery and reply practices.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender should be able to learn whether a fax was delivered, not delivered or could not be confirmed. The protocol should also let different devices work together even when they have different capabilities.

sections.title: Functional Goals
sections.content:
Image formats should be widely used and able to represent commonly used traditional fax compression methods. Transmission must work across the Internet, intranets and firewalls. Addressing must reach Internet Fax devices, traditional fax terminals and email addresses.

The source of a fax must be identified, and a normal email reply should be possible for fax delivered by email. A standard should provide a uniform way to express sender and recipient capabilities. Capability statements sent separately from a message should identify who they concern and when they apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol should use image formats and addresses that different systems can understand. It should also identify senders and give devices a clear way to describe what they can receive.

sections.title: Security and Other Risks
sections.content:
An Internet Fax protocol must address the security goals in the memo. It should avoid causing harm through automatic notifications or capability exchange, which could expose users to message loops, repeated delivery or denial of service. It should not reveal private information by default.

The memo says users expect privacy and integrity comparable to telephone-based fax. Interoperation with traditional fax security and Internet email security is desirable. The protocol must state how it provides the security features users expect.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet Fax should protect the privacy and integrity users expect from fax. Automatic replies and capability messages must also be designed so they do not create new problems.
